compensating.why: hop 1 runs a second pass over the interfaces found
hop 2 puts the class's own interfaces into the type list
hop 4 calls a second time over the interfaces found

ownership_reason: Only the gold visits the types together with their interfaces; hop 1 copies a set into a list, hop 2 lists the class and its superclasses, hops 3 and 4 hand the types along. The gold adds the interfaces of every type before it returns, so anything a hop adds afterwards is appended after IA and cannot restore the documented order [IB, IC, ID, IE, IF, IA]; reaching the interfaces an interface extends needs a recursive walk, which no production utility other than the facade itself offers. The convention is pinned outside the gold: the facade's javadoc (each interface followed up its hierarchy, then each superclass, later duplicates ignored); MethodUtils.getAccessibleMethodFromInterfaceNest recursively checks the parent interfaces of each interface of a class and its superclasses; FieldUtils.getField and ClassUtils.getPublicMethod consume the list (FieldUtilsTest.testGetField finds Foo through the package-private superclass Parent, testAmbig needs both Foo and Bar, ClassUtilsTest.testGetPublicMethod finds isEmpty on a public interface); ClassUtilsTest.test_getAllSuperclasses_Class pins the type order hop 2 builds on. The gold's own contract is violated on the trigger: a class implements every interface its declared interfaces extend (CY is an ID, IE and IF through IC), and the gold returns without adding them. Recorded bypass (test-fitted): hop 4 calling the gold once per type and then recursing through itself over each declared interface passes the full suite, but it re-implements the traversal outside the gold and breaks the facade's documented order: for C implements I1, I2 with I1 extends J it lists I1, I2, J, while the correct chain lists I1, J, I2 (each interface followed up its hierarchy before the next).
